  1329  C. Establishing the Optional Practical Training Fees
  1330  
  1331      After considering the problematic issues plaguing the practical 
  1332  training programs in recent years and substantial rise in participants, 
  1333  as discussed above in section IV.A-C, DHS believes that program fees 
  1334  are necessary for all types of OPT. DHS believes that its mission in 
  1335  combating fraud, as well as protecting U.S. workers and upholding the 
  1336  integrity of the immigration system, would be furthered through a fee, 
  1337  which would deter the participation by adverse actors and increase the 
  1338  level of oversight and scrutiny by schools when endorsing OPT for its 
  1339  students.
  1340      As noted above, DHS believes that absent these fees, it will not be 
  1341  able to operate OPT consistent with its focus on preventing fraud and 
  1342  protecting American workers and may shut down the program entirely.
  1343      Specifically, DHS believes this proposed fee would incentivize 
  1344  educational institutions to exercise greater oversight and selectivity 
  1345  when recommending students for OPT, thereby reducing fraudulent 
  1346  authorizations and curbing ``visa mill'' activities. By establishing a 
  1347  financial obligation through a fee, this proposed rule would encourage 
  1348  schools to ensure that OPT opportunities provide genuine educational 
  1349  value that aligns with the original intent of the practical training 
  1350  program, thereby promoting shared responsibility and accountability. 
  1351  Schools would have a direct stake in the integrity of the OPT program, 
  1352  incentivizing them to strengthen their internal compliance and 
  1353  selection processes and only issue OPT recommendations to those 
  1354  students for whom the school will pay the required fee. The financial 
  1355  costs would deter schools from recommending students with questionable 
  1356  qualifications for OPT, leading to higher program integrity. DHS 
  1357  anticipates that schools will consider adopting internal policies and 
  1358  procedures that prioritize quality and compliance over quantity of 
  1359  participants, stabilizing the number of OPT participants. This fee 
  1360  would result in a smaller pool of participants, as schools would be 
  1361  more selective in determining which students are qualified to 
  1362  participate in OPT. In turn, the rule, as proposed, would effectively 
  1363  eliminate students who engage in OPT as a pathway for low-paid 
  1364  employment or those who are trying to circumvent the H-1B visa cap and 
  1365  fee requirements, as they would no longer be able to obtain 
  1366  ``automatic'' recommendations for OPT from their schools. DHS believes 
  1367  that this proposed fee would incentivize schools to only recommend the 
  1368  most promising students to engage in OPT after a thorough review and 
  1369  payment of the required fee. Limiting the pool of OPT participants to 
  1370  talented students who are in genuine educational programs and placed in 
  1371  training programs that directly relate to their major area of study 
  1372  would protect the interests and jobs of American workers in the long 
  1373  run. The proposed rule would alleviate the job market from depressed 
  1374  wages and low-paid jobs otherwise held by F-1 nonimmigrant students. 
  1375  Additionally, the proposed rule would curb the number of students and 
  1376  employers attempting to circumvent the H-1B visa cap and fee, and thus, 
  1377  result in less replacement of U.S. workers, as schools would have 
  1378  greater equity and stake than employers in determining who participates 
  1379  in OPT due to their financial responsibilities.
  1380      A reduction in the pool of OPT applicants, along with the 
  1381  stabilization of participant numbers, would alleviate DHS's resource 
  1382  burden tied to enforcement activities related to OPT and enable the 
  1383  agency to conduct more focused and efficient oversight of SEVP 
  1384  programs. Enhanced school compliance would reduce the investigative and 
  1385  enforcement burden on DHS, allowing limited resources to be focused on 
  1386  higher-priority cases. Specifically, it would allow SEVP to 
  1387  strategically allocate resources to other programs that it administers 
  1388  and regulates. With fewer applicants to monitor, SEVP would be able to 
  1389  focus its investigative efforts on high-risk industries and sectors 
  1390  where OPT abuse is more likely to occur, such as technology and 
  1391  critical infrastructure. This targeted approach would enable
  1392  
  1393  [[Page 64575]]
  1394  
  1395  more thorough reviews of participating students and schools, while 
  1396  freeing up personnel to support other programs managed by SEVP, 
  1397  including OPT and CPT, and provide heightened customer service and 
  1398  technical support to educational institutions and other stakeholders. 
  1399  In turn, by streamlining operational planning and focusing resources 
  1400  where vulnerabilities are greatest, DHS would improve the quality and 
  1401  effectiveness of compliance checks, fraud detection, and enforcement 
  1402  actions, ultimately strengthening the integrity of the OPT program and 
  1403  related SEVP initiatives.
  1404      This streamlining and strategic allocation of DHS resources, 
  1405  combined with the reporting requirements under 20 U.S.C. 1011f of the 
  1406  Higher Education Act that are already in place will enable law 
  1407  enforcement to detect, analyze, and investigate suspicious financial 
  1408  transactions tied to foreign governments or threat actors that may seek 
  1409  to use OPT to steal US technology or advance other national security 
  1410  threats. Generally, schools would need to track how they are funding 
  1411  the OPT fees in their financial reports and disclosures for accounting 
  1412  purposes. These reporting and accounting mechanisms could aid law 
  1413  enforcement in tracking the origin and purpose of the funds. Since the 
  1414  funding of OPT participation is costly and requires transparency, the 
  1415  OPT fee could expose attempts by foreign adversaries to subsidize these 
  1416  costs through targeted investments or donations to schools offering OPT 
  1417  to F-1 nonimmigrant students. For example, large or unusual financial 
  1418  contributions from foreign sources, especially those tied to programs 
  1419  that rely heavily on OPT, could serve as red flags for further 
  1420  investigation into fraud and national security concerns.
  1421      Furthermore, INA 274A(h)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324a(h)(1), notes that, 
  1422  ``[i]n providing documentation or endorsement of authorization of 
  1423  aliens . . . authorized to be employed in the United States, the 
  1424  Attorney General shall provide that any limitations with respect to the 
  1425  period or type of employment or employer shall be conspicuously stated 
  1426  on the documentation or endorsement.'' As such, DHS believes the 
  1427  financial obligation of the proposed fee, in tandem with the 
  1428  requirement that SEVP-certified institutions provide proof of payment 
  1429  of this fee when submitting a recommendation for OPT, also serves as a 
  1430  deterrent to schools, foreign students, and employers seeking to abuse 
  1431  OPT.
  1432      DHS believes that this proposed rule does not need to define which 
  1433  OPT experiences provide genuine educational value that is directly 
  1434  related to the F-1 nonimmigrant student's major area of study, given 
  1435  that the current regulations provide the eligibility framework for OPT 
  1436  and schools are in a better position to assess the weight and value of 
  1437  hands-on educational programs offered through OPT. Moreover, this 
  1438  proposed fee rule does not propose the imposition of specific 
  1439  limitations or restrictions on how the schools should collect or source 
  1440  the requisite funds to make the fee payments for each student engaged 
  1441  in OPT, to the extent that the school complies with all other 
  1442  applicable laws, including reporting foreign gifts and contracts under 
  1443  20 U.S.C. 1011f. DHS acknowledges that the schools may pass the 
  1444  financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant 
  1445  students, all students, or employers. If the proposed fee is passed on 
  1446  to F-1 nonimmigrant students or employers, it would further discourage 
  1447  misuse of OPT by increasing the cost of participation for those whose 
  1448  intent is primarily to work or reside in the U.S. without legitimate 
  1449  academic purpose and for employers displacing U.S. workers.
  1450      While DHS understands that the proposed fees are not nominal 
  1451  amounts, such costs are reasonably related to the purposes of INA 
  1452  101(a)(15)(F)(i), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(F)(i),\114\ and this proposed 
  1453  rule which addresses the vulnerabilities of OPT. Furthermore, these 
  1454  fees are intended to discourage aliens from using the OPT program to 
  1455  market themselves to employers seeking to bypass H-1B caps, fees, and 
  1456  prevailing wage requirements. In weighing the educational costs and the 
  1457  value of hands-on training experience in the United States, DHS 
  1458  believes that the OPT fees are on par with the educational costs that 
  1459  foreign students incur for one or two years of education in a program 
  1460  of study in the United States. However, DHS acknowledges that there may 
  1461  be instances in which a refund of the payment is necessary when OPT 
  1462  does not proceed as initially intended. The proposed rule includes 
  1463  refund provisions so that educational institutions may seek a refund if 
  1464  the student does not receive an OPT employment authorization document.
  1465  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1466  
  1467      \114\ See Narenji, 617 F.2d at 745.
  1468  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1469  
  1470      The proposed rule intends for schools to pay the applicable fees 
  1471  for eligible students who will engage in a form of OPT, regardless of 
  1472  the manner in which the foreign student obtained F-1 status--whether 
  1473  admitted in F-1 status or through a change of status (COS) within the 
  1474  United States--and irrespective of how the F-1 student obtained an 
  1475  extension of stay when seeking to engage in a form of OPT. In other 
  1476  words, the proposed fee would apply equally for all schools and 
  1477  students seeking to engage in OPT, regardless of whether the F-1 
  1478  student received an Extension of Stay (EOS) authorization through USCIS 
  1479  or through CBP after traveling abroad to obtain a new I-94 to engage in 
  1480  OPT.
  1481      DHS proposes to establish two different OPT fee amounts. DHS 
  1482  believes that the initial OPT fee amount should be higher than the 
  1483  subsequent fee amounts because, when nonimmigrant students initially 
  1484  apply for employment authorization, they may not have been vetted by 
  1485  the U.S. Government since their initial application for an F-1 visa and 
  1486  subsequent admission into the country.\115\ The importance of ensuring 
  1487  integrity in the OPT program is most prevalent at this stage. For the 
  1488  initial fee, DHS also considered the possibility that nonimmigrants 
  1489  could undermine the H-1B visa payment by abusing OPT.\116\ As such, DHS 
  1490  selected a fee amount for OPT comparable to the fee for H-1B visas 
  1491  \117\ that would deter visa fraud. The fee amount is designed to 
  1492  closely align with the H-1B fees to reduce students and employers from 
  1493  using OPT to circumvent the H-1B visa program fees. Schools would have 
  1494  to pay the OPT fee prior to the DSO entering the recommendation for OPT 
  1495  in SEVIS. To be clear, no DSO would be able to enter an OPT 
  1496  recommendation without the school having paid the applicable fee. 
  1497  Through this rule, DHS intends to verify whether the schools have made 
  1498  OPT fee payments for each student that they recommend for OPT,
  1499  
  1500  [[Page 64576]]
  1501  
  1502  thereby strengthening the integrity of the program.
  1503  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1504  
  1505      \115\ DHS recognizes that the application requirements for EOS 
  1506  under 8 CFR 214.1(c) and 214.2(f)(7)(v) may provide DHS with 
  1507  additional opportunities to vet F-1 nonimmigrant students. See 
  1508  ``Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of 
  1509  Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange 
  1510  Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media,'' 91 FR 
  1511  44976 (July 17, 2026). This final rule (hereinafter ``Duration of 
  1512  Status Final Rule'') amended the admission period for F nonimmigrant 
  1513  classification from duration of status to a fixed time period and 
  1514  implemented additional changes to admission and extension 
  1515  requirements. However, not all F-1 nonimmigrant students are 
  1516  required to apply for an EOS to engage OPT, such as those 
  1517  participating in pre-completion OPT or those grandfathered under the 
  1518  Duration of Status Final Rule and subject to the regulations at 8 
  1519  CFR 214.2(m). DHS believes that the regulations currently in effect, 
  1520  together with the proposed OPT fee rule, will provide a 
  1521  comprehensive and holistic approach for DHS to effectively regulate 
  1522  the OPT program.
  1523      \116\ See Proclamation No. 10973, 90 FR (Sept. 19, 2025), 
  1524  Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.
  1525      \117\ Id.
  1526  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1527  
  1528      Notably, the proposed OPT fees collected under this rule would be 
  1529  deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous 
  1530  receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302. ICE would not maintain or use the 
  1531  funding collected under these OPT fee provisions promulgated pursuant 
  1532  to INA 214(a), 8 U.S.C. 1184, because the statute does not provide 
  1533  legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected. While the OPT 
  1534  fees would be deposited into the Treasury of the United States and not 
  1535  specifically earmarked for ICE SEVP or immigration enforcement 
  1536  activities, the collection of these fees remain essential in addressing 
  1537  the vulnerabilities of the OPT program for the reasons explained in 
  1538  this section. It is also conceivable that funds collected could later 
  1539  be effectively appropriated by Congress to various government agencies 
  1540  to further enhance the integrity of the immigration system. However, 
  1541  the deterrent nature of the OPT fee remains regardless of whether these 
  1542  funds are appropriated by Congress to government agencies for this 
  1543  purpose.
  1544      DHS considered some alternative regulatory approaches to address 
  1545  the issues in OPT that were discussed in sections IV.A. and IV.B. of 
  1546  the rule, such as applying STEM OPT requirements like site visits, 
  1547  training plans, and additional reporting to OPT more generally. 
  1548  However, DHS ultimately determined that proposing a fee for 
  1549  participation in the OPT program would offer an immediate and effective 
  1550  means to strengthen the integrity of OPT with minimal administrative 
  1551  burdens on the government. Unlike more complex regulatory alternatives, 
  1552  such as expanded site visits, increased reporting requirements, 
  1553  additional processes, and stricter procedural mandates, a fee can be 
  1554  implemented quickly and uniformly across all participants. This 
  1555  approach does not require DHS to deploy significant additional 
  1556  resources for enforcement or oversight. Moreover, the effect of a 
  1557  financial commitment is nearly immediate--those seeking to abuse the 
  1558  program are less likely to invest in participation when faced with a 
  1559  tangible cost, making engagement in OPT for nefarious purposes less 
  1560  attractive to bad actors. Furthermore, the financial commitment of this 
  1561  fee may encourage schools to apply a heightened level of scrutiny when 
  1562  reviewing an F-1 nonimmigrant student's request for OPT to ensure that 
  1563  the student is engaging in a legitimate OPT opportunity.
  1564      Although STEM OPT has regulatory safeguards, including reporting 
  1565  obligations, employer site visits, and the Form I-983 training plan 
  1566  requirement, DHS does not believe that simply extending those 
  1567  requirements to the initial period of post-completion OPT would be 
  1568  sufficient as an initial response to the overarching OPT program 
  1569  integrity concerns. Experience with STEM OPT indicates that additional 
  1570  procedural and documentation requirements, while useful, do not 
  1571  eliminate the risk of fraud, abuse, or noncompliance and may require 
  1572  substantial time and resources to implement, monitor, and enforce 
  1573  effectively. Solutions requiring self-attestations, reporting, or 
  1574  reliance on an honor system, without more, are insufficient to ensure 
  1575  the integrity of the OPT program. These mechanisms would need to be 
  1576  paired with enforcement activity, such as conducting more site visits 
  1577  across a broader range of employers, which may function less as a 
  1578  proactive fraud-prevention measure and more as reactive response to 
  1579  violations after they occur. In contrast, by requiring a financial 
  1580  commitment through an OPT fee, DHS would encourage participant to 
  1581  demonstrate a seriousness and genuine intent to comply with program 
  1582  requirements. The fee establishes a tangible stake in the process, 
  1583  helping to distinguish those who are committed to lawful participation 
  1584  from those who may seek to exploit the program. In addition to the 
  1585  current regulatory mechanisms in place, this additional layer of 
  1586  accountability supports the Department's broader efforts to uphold the 
  1587  integrity and effectiveness of the OPT program.
  1588      The Department recognizes the importance of restoring and 
  1589  maintaining public confidence in the OPT program through an immediate, 
  1590  effective regulatory solution, rather than a complex bureaucratic 
  1591  framework that may take years to yield results. By proposing a fee, 
  1592  rather than alternative administrative procedures, the Department seeks 
  1593  to minimize overregulation and complexities while responding to serious 
  1594  program integrity concerns that cannot be addressed quickly through 
  1595  such procedures alone. Recent concerns regarding misuse and fraud and 
  1596  the displacement of American workers have underscored the need for 
  1597  visible, effective action to reinforce the integrity of the program. 
  1598  The fee serves as a clear signal to the public and stakeholders that 
  1599  the Department is taking meaningful steps to safeguard the OPT program, 
  1600  while ensuring that legitimate participants continue to benefit from 
  1601  its opportunities.
  1602      DHS believes the OPT fee is a crucial first step to urgently 
  1603  address fraud, abuse, and noncompliance, in a targeted and immediately 
  1604  implementable manner. This measured approach allows for ongoing 
  1605  evaluation of the fee's impact and effectiveness, providing the agency 
  1606  with valuable data to inform future policy decisions. Importantly, the 
  1607  implementation of a fee should not be interpreted as precluding future 
  1608  changes to the OPT program through additional regulatory requirements; 
  1609  rather, it represents an immediate first step in a graduated strategy 
  1610  to address the urgent program integrity concerns. The Department seeks 
  1611  to retain flexibility to pursue additional regulatory measures in the 
  1612  future should further action be warranted.
  1613      In considering fees, DHS carefully evaluated various fee options, 
  1614  including exemptions to the fee for small educational institutions. See 
  1615  sec. VII.B.6. However, DHS estimates that 56 percent of regulated SEVP-
  1616  certified institutions are small entities. Id. This approach could 
  1617  leave significant fraud vulnerabilities unaddressed, given that many 
  1618  SEVP-certified institutions are small entities. Various factors and 
  1619  data were considered in this proposed rule, as explained in section 
  1620  VII.B.6.
  1621      Separately, DHS acknowledges that OPT is not the only practical 
  1622  training program with the potential for significant fraud and national 
  1623  security issues. Fraud and national security threats in CPT have also

  1643  V. Discussion of Changes
  1644  
  1645  A. Establishing a Fee for Initial and Any Subsequent OPT
  1646  
  1647      The proposed rule would establish a fee of $70,000 per F-1 
  1648  nonimmigrant
  1649  
  1650  [[Page 64577]]
  1651  
  1652  student applicable to SEVP-certified schools that recommend an F-1 
  1653  nonimmigrant student to engage in OPT for the first time. See proposed 
  1654  8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and 214.13(i)(1). This fee amount would apply to 
  1655  any type of OPT that the student participates in for the first time 
  1656  (irrespective of whether it is pre-completion OPT or post-completion 
  1657  OPT). Id. The initial $70,000 is a one-time fee that an SEVP-certified 
  1658  educational institution must pay for each F-1 nonimmigrant student 
  1659  prior to a DSO's initial recommendation of an F-1 nonimmigrant student 
  1660  to participate in any type of OPT under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii) for the 
  1661  first time. To be clear, this OPT fee would not be tied to a specific 
  1662  employer; rather the OPT fee would be applicable when a school decides 
  1663  to recommend an F-1 nonimmigrant student for any type of OPT.
  1664      The proposed rule would also establish a fee of $30,000 per F-1 
  1665  nonimmigrant student applicable to SEVP-certified schools that make any 
  1666  subsequent OPT recommendation for an F-1 nonimmigrant student who has 
  1667  previously participated in OPT and has previously paid the initial OPT 
  1668  fee of $70,000. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2). As such, this 
  1669  subsequent $30,000 fee would apply to any type of OPT that an F-1 
  1670  nonimmigrant student participates in after having completed their 
  1671  initial OPT (regardless of whether it is another pre-completion OPT, 
  1672  post-completion OPT, or STEM OPT extension). Id. The OPT fee is not 
  1673  triggered by a change in employer but rather a school's decision to 
  1674  recommend a student for any type of OPT. For example, if an F-1 
  1675  nonimmigrant student obtains a DSO recommendation for pre-completion 
  1676  OPT and completes the training, they would need to obtain a subsequent 
  1677  DSO recommendation for post-completion OPT, regardless of whether the 
  1678  employer is the same for post-completion OPT and pre-completion OPT. In 
  1679  this instance, the school would need to pay $70,000 for the student's 
  1680  pre-completion OPT and $30,000 for the student's post-completion OPT. 
  1681  As with the initial OPT fee, the subsequent OPT fee would need to be 
  1682  paid for the F-1 nonimmigrant student prior to the DSO entering the OPT 
  1683  recommendation in SEVIS. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii). 
  1684  Additionally, USCIS would not grant employment authorization to any 
  1685  student prior to payment of the applicable OPT fee for the student. See 
  1686  proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii).
  1687      The proposed rule reiterates that the schools must pay the 
  1688  applicable OPT fees prior to the DSO entering the OPT recommendation 
  1689  for an F-1 nonimmigrant student in SEVIS. See proposed 8 CFR 
  1690  214.2(f)(11)(i)-(ii), 214.13(i). A DSO may not enter the OPT 
  1691  recommendation in SEVIS if the OPT fee has not yet been paid. The 
  1692  proposed rule requires the DSO to confirm that the school has paid the 
  1693  applicable OPT fee prior to updating SEVIS with the DSO's 
  1694  recommendation and before the student can apply to USCIS for employment 
  1695  authorization. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)(B). The DSO would 
  1696  need to provide the F-1 nonimmigrant student with a new I-20 with the 
  1697  DSO's recommendation and OPT fee payment information so that the 
  1698  student may file the Form I-765 with USCIS. See proposed 8 CFR 
  1699  214.2(f)(11)(i), (ii)(C). The proposed rule provides that USCIS would 
  1700  not grant employment authorization to any student where the school has 
  1701  failed to pay the applicable OPT fee prior to issuing an OPT 
  1702  recommendation or in instances where the school has completely failed 
  1703  to pay the applicable OPT fees. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii).
  1704      For the initial OPT fees, the proposed rule provides that a school 
  1705  may request a refund if the F-1 nonimmigrant student has not received 
  1706  an employment authorization document for OPT for which the payment has 
  1707  been made. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1). The proposed rule makes 
  1708  clear that this fee would not be refunded under any circumstances once 
  1709  the F-1 nonimmigrant student has received an employment authorization 
  1710  document for OPT. Id. Similarly, for subsequent OPT fees, the proposed 
  1711  rule provides that a school may request refund if the student has not 
  1712  received an employment authorization document for OPT or an OPT 
  1713  extension. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2). The DSO would need to 
  1714  remove the F-1 nonimmigrant student's OPT recommendation in SEVIS 
  1715  before requesting a refund. For all refund requests, SEVP would review 
  1716  each request on a case-by-case basis and exercise discretion in 
  1717  adjudicating the request. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2). The 
  1718  proposed rule also provides that SEVP may consider providing further 
  1719  guidance on its website regarding the refund request adjudication. Id. 
  1720  SEVP's determination on the refund request would be final and not 
  1721  appealable. Id.
  1722      DHS has also considered, as an alternative to the approach 
  1723  described above, having the one-time initial fee of $70,000 apply again 
  1724  to any initial period of OPT following the F-1 student's change to a 
  1725  higher educational level (e.g., to a post-bachelor's degree OPT and 
  1726  again to the student's master's degree OPT). DHS welcomes public 
  1727  comments on the rule in its entirety but especially encourages input 
  1728  from the public on this potential alternative.
  1729  
  1730  B. Technical Amendments
  1731  
  1732      Since an additional fee is being proposed within 8 CFR 214.13, DHS

   227  II. Executive Summary
   228  
   229  A. Purpose of Regulatory Action
   230  
   231      The purpose of this proposed rulemaking is to generate dedicated 
   232  revenue to support the costs of administering the lawful immigration 
   233  system. To achieve this result DHS has decided to establish an 
   234  additional fee on all H-1B cap-subject petitions, payable at the time 
   235  of filing. The new fee is designed, consistent with section 286(m) of 
   236  the Immigration and
   237  
   238  [[Page 54819]]
   239  
   240  Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1356(m), to recover a portion of the 
   241  full costs of providing immigration adjudication and naturalization 
   242  services incurred by multiple Federal agencies in processing, 
   243  adjudicating, and supporting the lawful immigration system, including 
   244  U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), U.S. Customs and 
   245  Border Protection (CBP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) 
   246  in DHS, Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) in DOJ, DOS, and 
   247  DOL.
   248      The lawful immigration system is largely funded by user fees.\1\ As 
   249  explained later in this rule, DHS's interagency cost assessments have 
   250  identified substantial activities that directly relate to the costs of 
   251  providing immigration adjudication and naturalization services across 
   252  the federal government, such as adjudications, associated 
   253  investigations, enforcement and vetting support, information technology 
   254  modernization and maintenance, records management, and interagency 
   255  coordination.\2\ The proposed H-1B fee is intended to provide a 
   256  powerful, reliable, and predictable revenue tool to address the costs 
   257  across multiple agencies that oversee the United States immigration 
   258  system.
   259  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   260  
   261      \1\ See, e.g., U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Fee 
   262  Schedule and Changes to Certain Other Immigration Benefit Request 
   263  Requirements, 89 FR 6194 (Jan. 31, 2024) (final rule).
   264      \2\ For more information, see section V.A. Cost Basis of this 
   265  preamble.
   266  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   267  
   268      DHS considered whether to propose recovery of the government's 
   269  lawful immigration-related costs by adding a fee to all immigration 
   270  benefit requests, or certain requests. We also considered increasing 
   271  the existing H-1B petition fee in 8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(i), rather than 
   272  establishing a separate H-1B fee provision. For the reasons provided in 
   273  this notice, DHS is proposing to add a fee at 8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(xii) 
   274  that would apply only to H-1B cap-subject petitions, including those 
   275  eligible for the advanced degree exemption (not to all H-1B petitions 
   276  such as cap-exempt filings).
   277      The proposed fee is specifically to recover the interagency costs 
   278  described in this rule and having a standalone fee is intended to 
   279  facilitate tracking, allocation, and reporting of the associated 
   280  revenue. For these reasons, DHS proposes to implement the $103,265 
   281  amount as a separate, additional H-1B fee rather than combining it with 
   282  the existing H-1B petition fee in 8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(i).
   283      The proposed fee, when required, would be in addition to any other 
   284  applicable fees or payments,\3\ including any separate payment 
   285  obligation required under a Presidential Proclamation.\4\ Accordingly, 
   286  to the extent a petitioner is subject both to a proclamation-required 
   287  payment and to the additional H-1B fee proposed in this rule, the 
   288  petitioner would be required to pay both amounts.
   289  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   290  
   291      \3\ See USCIS Form G-1055, Fee Schedule, https://www.uscis.gov/g-1055 (last reviewed/updated June 15, 2026), for a list of 
   292  applicable H-1B fees and payments; See also, Presidential 
   293  Proclamation 10973, ``Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant 
   294  Workers.'' 90 FR 46027 (Sept. 19, 2025). The proposed fee in this 
   295  NPRM would be an additional fee separate from the $100,000 payment 
   296  required by Proclamation 10973 and is based on different authority. 
   297  See Section III.A. of this NPRM for a detailed discussion of the 
   298  authority for this proposed fee. The payment required by the 
   299  Proclamation as a restriction on entry based on sections 212(f) and

    50  I. Background
    51  
    52  A. Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
    53  
    54      On June 6, 2024, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) 
    55  published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) in the Federal

    64  
    65  1. Initial Supplemental H-1B and L-1 Fee
    66      H-1B and L-1 visa classifications are temporary nonimmigrant worker

    87  Specialty Occupations, DOD Cooperative Research and Development

    97  Public Law 111-230, 124 Stat. 2485, 2487 (hereinafter Pub. L. 111-230) 
    98  (8 U.S.C. 1101 note). The 2010 Supplemental Fee applied to employers 
    99  that employ 50 or more total employees in the United States with more 
   100  than 50 percent of the employees in the United States in H-1B or L-1 
   101  nonimmigrant status (covered employers). Sec. 402, Public Law 111-230. 
   102  For these covered employers, the statute stated ``the filing fee and 
   103  fraud prevention and detection fee [. . .] shall be increased by $2,000

summary.text:
**Evaluating filing fees**

I find it interesting how the budget is reducing quickly despite a large amount, like 95k. I need to clarify the I539 filing fee, which is currently $420 for e-filing and $470 for paper filing. I'm checking if these figures are accurate based on the 2024 final rule. If there's a statute update coming, it could raise the fee to $500. I should confirm this by searching the federal register for the correct details about 8 CFR 106 I539.

  5265  E. Calculation of Admission Periods, Grace Periods, and Dependents
  5266  
  5267  1. Early Program Completion Grace Periods
  5268      Comments: A commenter requested clarification on the final deciding 
  5269  factor on the program end date and start date of the F-1 nonimmigrant 
  5270  grace period under the proposed rule, particularly if an F-1 student 
  5271  completes their program earlier than the I-20 program end date and Form 
  5272  I-94 admission end date. Commenters stated the 30-day period does not 
  5273  provide enough time for students to book flights where availability is 
  5274  limited nor is it enough time to attain employment. Specifically the 
  5275  commenter outlined two scenarios: (1) a student's Form I-20 lists a 
  5276  program end date of May 31, 2027, but the student actually completes 
  5277  coursework on May 15, 2027; and (2) a student is admitted with a Form 
  5278  I-20 end date of May 31, 2027, and a matching AUD on the Form I-94; 
  5279  however, due to advanced credits and summer coursework, the student 
  5280  completes the program a full year earlier on May 15, 2026.
  5281      Response: DHS agrees on the importance of maximizing the period of 
  5282  admission to apply toward the F-1 nonimmigrants' program of study. DHS 
  5283  appreciates the commenter's request for clarification on the grace 
  5284  period and how to resolve instances when a student completes their 
  5285  program of study before the expiration date listed on the Form I-94.
  5286  
  5287  [[Page 45016]]
  5288  
  5289      The rule provides that the 30-day period before the indicated 
  5290  report date or program start date and the 30 additional days (grace 
  5291  period) following the program end date, or the 4-year maximum period of 
  5292  admission, do not count toward the maximum length of stay. See new 8 
  5293  CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i). Specifically, the calculation of the 4-year maximum 
  5294  periods of admission would not begin from the date of admission during 
  5295  the initial 30-day window, but from the program start date. Similarly, 
  5296  the 30-day departure period would not count towards the 4-year maximum 
  5297  period of admission. This will mitigate scenarios where an F-1 student 
  5298  is in need of an EOS because their admission period is 30 days short 
  5299  from the 4-year program completion date.
  5300      With respect to programs ending earlier than the date on the I-94, 
  5301  a nonimmigrant student's period of admission is granted to the program 
  5302  of study on Form I-20, for a maximum of four years, plus an additional 
  5303  30-days period for departure. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (v). When a 
  5304  student completes their program prior to the program end date as listed 
  5305  on the Form I-20, the DSO should shorten the date in SEVIS, and the 
  5306  student will have 30 days to depart the country after their program 
  5307  completion, regardless of the initial admission date provided on Form 
  5308  I-94. The final rule adds a provision to clarify this point, by stating 
  5309  that ``if the F-1 student ends his or her study or training prior to 
  5310  expiration of his or her period of admission, the F-1 student, and any 
  5311  eligible dependents, must, within 30 days from the end date of the 
  5312  study or training, depart the United States or otherwise seek to 
  5313  maintain lawful status.'' See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).
  5314  2. Fixed Admission Period Start and End Dates
  5315      Comments: A commenter requested clarification on the date from 
  5316  which the fixed period of admission will be calculated for F-1 
  5317  students, if the proposed rule is finalized. Specifically, the 
  5318  commenters stated that the preamble text and proposed regulatory text 
  5319  do not distinguish between the Program Start Date (or ``report date''), 
  5320  and the Initial Session Start Date, which the commenters noted are 
  5321  recorded separately in SEVIS and displayed separately on the I-20. The 
  5322  commenters also expressed appreciation for the ability to set a Program 
  5323  Start Date earlier than the actual start of classes but requested that 
  5324  DHS consider calculating the period of fixed admission from the Initial 
  5325  Session Start Date, which the commenters stated is the actual start of 
  5326  classes for the program of study. The commenters reasoned that this 
  5327  would ensure that F-1 students who are admitted for a fixed period of 
  5328  admission can maximally use that period of admission toward their 
  5329  program of study.
  5330      Response: DHS appreciates this opportunity to clarify how this

  5337  start date, but those days will not be taken into account when 
  5338  calculating the maximum allowed period of stay. Upon admission into the 
  5339  United States, a fixed period of stay is granted up to the program end 
  5340  date, not to exceed 4 years, plus an additional 30-days for F and J 
  5341  nonimmigrants to depart. DHS appreciates the suggested alternatives 
  5342  provided by the commenters, but DHS believes the regulatory text is 
  5343  clear and that no additional clarification is needed as the final rule 
  5344  will achieve the same desired result as what the commenters were 
  5345  suggesting.
  5346  3. Dependent Admission Periods
  5347      Comments: A commenter requested clarification on what would happen 
  5348  under the proposed changes if a nonimmigrant student traveled 
  5349  separately from their F-2 dependent, the nonimmigrant student's status 
  5350  is shortened upon re-entry, and the F-2's Form I-94 reflects a longer 
  5351  end date.
  5352      Response: The current regulation requiring the spouse and minor 
  5353  children of an F-1 student to individually present a Form I-20 or 
  5354  successor form, whether accompanying or following-to-join the F-1 
  5355  student has not been impacted by this rule. DHS notes that under new 8 
  5356  CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E), the authorized period of stay for F-2 dependents 
  5357  may not exceed the authorized period of stay of the principal F-1 
  5358  student. Dependents must file for an EOS when the principal does, 
  5359  cannot stay longer than the principal, and must depart if the EOS is 
  5360  denied. If the principal's stay is shortened, then the dependents must 
  5361  depart at the same time as the principal even if their I-94 has a 
  5362  longer period of stay.
  5363

  5745  G. EOS
  5746  
  5747  1. EOS Regulations, Process, and Requirements
  5748  a. Concerns About Potential Drafting Error or Unjustified Change to 
  5749  Form I-129 Deference Policy
  5750      Comments: Commenters noted that the proposed technical amendment to 
  5751  section.214.1(c)(5) was not merely technical, as described in the 
  5752  preamble, but would represent a substantive shift that would increase 
  5753  burdens, reduce adjudicatory efficiency, and introduce inconsistency. 
  5754  Commenters stated that
  5755  
  5756  [[Page 45020]]
  5757  
  5758  striking all references to Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant 
  5759  Worker, and Form I-539, Application to Change/Extend Nonimmigrant 
  5760  Status from 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) would result in the repeal of the current 
  5761  regulatory mandate for USCIS adjudicators to give deference to prior 
  5762  agency determinations involving the same employer and employee when 
  5763  there are no material factual changes. They reasoned this would 
  5764  increase financial and administrative burdens, narrow flexibility, 
  5765  create risks of inconsistent adjudications, and result in unnecessary 
  5766  re-adjudication of petitions. Some commenters also argued this change 
  5767  was outside the scope of the rule and not relevant to F, J, or I 
  5768  regulations.
  5769      Commenters further stated that the proposed change could be 
  5770  arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 
  5771  lacking reasoned explanation or adequate opportunity for public 
  5772  comment. Some believed the change was likely a drafting error, as the 
  5773  deference issue was not discussed in the preamble and the NPRM may have 
  5774  referenced an outdated version of the regulation.
  5775      Response: DHS appreciates the commenters' concerns and notes that 
  5776  the NPRM mistakenly cited 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) instead of 8 CFR 
  5777  241.1(c)(7). DHS now recognizes that a 2024 rulemaking had in fact 
  5778  renumbered the provision on decisions for EOS applications as 8 CFR 
  5779  214.1(c)(7) and had further made technical revisions to the provision, 
  5780  including removal of the specific form numbers.\164\ Accordingly, the 
  5781  revisions proposed in the NPRM related to 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) are no 
  5782  longer needed and will not be finalized in this rule. As such, DHS will 
  5783  not address substantive comments about the impact of the elimination of 
  5784  deference as those are outside of the scope of what DHS intended.
  5785  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  5786  
  5787      \164\ See Modernizing H-1B Requirements, Providing Flexibility 
  5788  in the F-1 Program, and Program Improvements Affecting Other 
  5789  Nonimmigrant Workers, 89 FR 103054 (Dec. 18, 2024).
  5790  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  5791  
  5792  b. General Feedback on the Requirement To File an EOS
  5793      Comments: Commenters stated that the proposed rule would increase 
  5794  administrative burden, uncertainty, and inefficiency. The shift to a 
  5795  fixed-term admission would require hundreds of thousands of 
  5796  nonimmigrants, particularly those in longer programs or pursuing OPT, 
  5797  to apply for EOS. Commenters noted that this could disrupt research, 
  5798  dissertations, teaching assistantships, and funding cycles; waste 
  5799  resources; and create duplicative review processes, especially since 
  5800  schools and SEVIS already monitor compliance. Concerns were raised 
  5801  about the risk of denials due to technical errors or AI-based 
  5802  adjudication. Some commenters said that each additional filing 
  5803  increases the risk of record mismatches or clerical errors, and that 
  5804  incomplete or misfiled forms would become more difficult to address in 
  5805  a system involving multiple agencies and forms. Commenters also cited 
  5806  significant economic contributions of foreign students and warned that 
  5807  the rule could reduce U.S. competitiveness and university revenues.
  5808      Response: DHS does not believe that establishing a fixed time 
  5809  period of authorized stay places undue burdens on F, J, and I 
  5810  nonimmigrants. F-1 students may apply for an EOS if they require 
  5811  additional time under their F-1 status, and the rulemaking includes a 
  5812  transition period for students currently on D/S, allowing for an 
  5813  orderly transition. Providing a fixed time period of authorized stay 
  5814  that requires application for extension, change of status, or other 
  5815  authorization is consistent with most other nonimmigrant 
  5816  classifications and with practices prior to 1979. While DHS 
  5817  acknowledges that this rule will impose additional burdens on some 
  5818  populations, the benefit to program integrity and national security 
  5819  outweighs the burdens.
  5820      Requiring F, J, and I nonimmigrants to request additional periods 
  5821  of admission directly with DHS will improve consistency, enable 
  5822  stronger oversight, and deter fraud and abuse. DHS acknowledges the 
  5823  economic contribution of foreign students and expects the United States 
  5824  to remain a competitive destination. The rule's potential impact on 
  5825  enrollment is discussed qualitatively in the economic analysis portion 
  5826  of this rule due to the speculative nature of the magnitude of any 
  5827  decrease.
  5828      DHS also appreciates commenters' concerns regarding the potential 
  5829  for technical errors and the use of automated or AI-based adjudication 
  5830  in the processing of immigration benefits under this rule. Requests for 
  5831  admission, extensions of stay, changes of status, and employment 
  5832  authorizations will continue to be adjudicated by trained DHS officers 
  5833  who apply statutory and regulatory requirements to the facts of each 
  5834  case. DHS is also conducting updates to SEVIS and updates to training 
  5835  to ensure a smooth transition and to minimize the risk of any technical 
  5836  errors. Further, USCIS, which is fee-funded, will continue to monitor 
  5837  its resource allocations and make adjustments as appropriate. DHS is 
  5838  committed to ensuring the integrity and fairness of the adjudication 
  5839  process and will continue to ensure appropriate safeguards are in 
  5840  place.
  5841  c. Impacts to the Immigration System or DHS
  5842  (1) Efficiency Concerns, Duplicative Processes, Backlogs, Delays, and 
  5843  USCIS Staffing
  5844      Comments: Commenters stated that the proposed rule would create 
  5845  duplicative processes within the immigration system, noting that 
  5846  nonimmigrants are already highly tracked and regulated. They argued the 
  5847  rule would create inefficiencies, confusion, costs, or risks, without 
  5848  demonstrating that D/S has failed or that the proposed rule would have 
  5849  beneficial outcomes. Some commenters said the rule would overwhelm 
  5850  USCIS with additional applications, exacerbating existing processing 
  5851  delays, and create a fragmented system with multiple agencies 
  5852  controlling separate parts of the process (DoS, CBP, DHS, USCIS). Many 
  5853  challenged DHS's estimate of 414,000 additional EOS applications 
  5854  annually, suggesting it was too low, and projected even higher numbers. 
  5855  Commenters also noted that DSOs would vet EOS applications before 
  5856  recommending an extension to DHS, resulting in duplicative review, and 
  5857  that the rule would force foreign students to navigate dual 
  5858  bureaucracies.
  5859      Commenters expressed concern that delays in processing EOS 
  5860  applications could have serious consequences for students and academic 
  5861  programs, including disruptions to research projects, teaching 
  5862  assignments, and clinical training. Doctoral programs and certain 
  5863  undergraduate programs that exceed four years would require at least 
  5864  one EOS application, creating uncertainty for students and 
  5865  institutions. Medical education and training pathways, which extend 
  5866  beyond four years, could also be negatively affected. Commenters 
  5867  expressed concerns that backlogs and delays in EOS applications would 
  5868  leave students and exchange visitors uncertain about their ability to 
  5869  remain in the country and continue their education, potentially 
  5870  disrupting enrollment, employment, stipends, and health insurance. They 
  5871  noted that such uncertainty could prompt status inquiries that would 
  5872  further exacerbate backlogs and could also impact hospitals and patient 
  5873  care. Commenters warned that delays would disrupt operations for 
  5874  students, institutions, businesses, embassies, and ports of
  5875  
  5876  [[Page 45021]]
  5877  
  5878  entry. Commenters noted spillover effects on other immigration benefits 
  5879  due to increased workload and cited research showing that processing 
  5880  delays could lead to job losses and reduced hiring. Commenters 
  5881  suggested setting a maximum adjudication timeline (e.g., 90 days) and 
  5882  reducing filing fees to minimize harm.
  5883      Response: The need for this rulemaking was discussed at length in 
  5884  the NPRM and is reiterated within this final rule. Fixed admission 
  5885  periods and periodic review will enhance compliance, reduce overstays, 
  5886  and improve national security and these benefits outweigh the effects. 
  5887  While the rule may cause an increase in USCIS processing times, DHS 
  5888  believes that the benefits of increased contact with these 
  5889  nonimmigrants outweigh processing time considerations. Requiring F, J, 
  5890  and I nonimmigrants to request an EOS will improve consistency of terms 
  5891  of admissions between nonimmigrant categories, enable stronger 
  5892  oversight by government officers who will review the nonimmigrant's 
  5893  request and assess compliance, and enhance the government's ability to 
  5894  enforce inadmissibility grounds related to unlawful presence.
  5895      DHS appreciates feedback on the estimated volume of additional EOS 
  5896  applications. DHS's estimates are modelled from historical data 
  5897  obtained from the SEVIS and ADIS systems, and the model has been 
  5898  updated with the most recent data sets. DHS will continue to evaluate 
  5899  actual application volumes and adjust resources and processes as 
  5900  necessary. USCIS, as a fee-funded agency, may set fees to support the 
  5901  additional workload and conduct comprehensive fee studies on a biennial 
  5902  basis, mitigating concerns about a spillover effect. USCIS will 
  5903  continue to monitor its resource allocations and make adjustments as 
  5904  appropriate. DHS also concludes that DSOs and ROs should no longer 
  5905  serve as direct proxies for immigration officers, though they will 
  5906  continue to perform important duties to assist DHS and nonimmigrant 
  5907  students. For example, commenters incorrectly assess that the work of 
  5908  the DSOs and ROs will be duplicative of that of USCIS or CBP. Quite on 
  5909  the contrary, it will be the DSOs and ROs who will decide if the 
  5910  program should be extended on academic or programmatic grounds. USCIS 
  5911  will determine if the nonimmigrant properly maintained status, has not 
  5912  abused the system, and is, therefore, eligible for an EOS. DHS 
  5913  understands that some programs of study may require additional time. 
  5914  The rule permits F, J, and I nonimmigrants who wish to remain in the 
  5915  United States beyond their specific authorized admission period to 
  5916  apply for authorization to extend their stay. Timely filed EOS 
  5917  applications allow students to remain in a period of authorized stay 
  5918  while pending, and automatic extension provisions help mitigate 
  5919  potential disruptions.
  5920      DHS appreciates the input regarding academic programs and 
  5921  employment opportunities that may be impacted and does not believe it 
  5922  is unreasonable to require aliens temporarily in the United States to 
  5923  file for an extension with USCIS to confirm compliance with U.S. 
  5924  immigration laws. Provisions in the rule allow F-1 and J-1 
  5925  nonimmigrants to continue their activities while EOS applications are 
  5926  pending, helping to prevent interruptions.
  5927      DHS recognizes concerns about potential duplicative review and the 
  5928  need for students to interact with multiple agencies. While DSOs and 
  5929  ROs continue to play a critical role in advising and supporting 
  5930  students, the rule is designed to ensure that final immigration status 
  5931  determinations are made by DHS officers, consistent with statutory 
  5932  requirements. DHS will work to provide clear guidance to minimize 
  5933  confusion and administrative burden.
  5934      DHS understands the importance of timely processing and strives to 
  5935  adjudicate applications as efficiently as possible. However, processing 
  5936  times can be affected by a variety of factors, including security 
  5937  vetting requirements, and the need for thorough review to ensure 
  5938  program integrity. That is why nonimmigrants are always encouraged and 
  5939  will continue to be encouraged to apply well in advance of the 
  5940  expiration of their stay so that their EOS can be timely adjudicated 
  5941  and not cause any disruption to their programs.

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

Abstract:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), proposes to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), which generally provides that USCIS gives deference to a prior approval involving the same facts when adjudicating a request to extend a petition for an alien's employment or stay. This change would better align DHS regulations with the statute, which places the burden of proving eligibility for all immigration benefits on the petitioner, applicant, or beneficiary; strengthen adjudicatory review; and support agency priorities to improve the integrity of the immigration system and better protect the interests of U.S. workers.

Abstract:
DHS is rescinding the 2022 public charge ground of inadmissibility regulations ("2022 Final Rule"). The 2022 Final Rule was not the best implementation of the statute. It was inconsistent with congressional intent, unduly restrictive, and hampered DHS's ability to make accurate, precise, and reliable determinations of whether certain aliens are likely at any time to become a public charge. Rescission restores broader discretion for DHS officers to evaluate all pertinent facts and aligns with long-standing policy that aliens in the United States should be self-reliant and government benefits should not incentivize immigration. This rule also revises the breach and cancellation of public charge bonds regulations.

Q2.answer: (a) Through July 14, 2027: May 15, 2027 I-20 end date + 60 days = July 14, 2027. This is the D/S transition arrangement in 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1), assuming Priya remains eligible and does not leave and receive a new fixed admission. (b) The outer transition dates stated in that provision are November 14, 2030 for F nonimmigrants and October 15, 2030 for J nonimmigrants: September 15, 2026 + four years = September 15, 2030; then + 60 or + 30 days, respectively. These are not a bar on a later, separately authorized extension. (c) Timing permits the August 24 start: May 15 + five months = October 15, 2027. The start must also be within five months of the transfer-out date; for an August 24 start, that date cannot be earlier than March 24, 2027. The earlier of the two five-month deadlines controls. (d) Yes. To remain for the new program, she needs a USCIS extension-of-stay application, currently Form I-539 or its successor, with the new properly endorsed I-20 and required fee. USCIS must receive a timely application before her current authorized stay expires. The transfer itself does not extend immigration stay. (e) On these alternative facts, she files Form I-765 for OPT but need not file Form I-539 for that requested OPT period: March 1, 2027 is before the express March 18 transition cutoff. If approved as requested, June 13, 2028 EAD expiration + 60 days = August 12, 2028.
Q2.basis: Final regulatory text: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1), (m)(1)(i), and (c)(2); 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B), (D), (f)(7)(iii)(B), (f)(8)(i)(G), (ii)–(iv), and (f)(10)(ii)(D), as amended by FR Doc. 2026-14439, 91 FR 45123–45127. The transition provision specifically requires an extension for a new program; the higher-level and transfer provisions supply additional support.
Q2.uncertainty: The transfer answer addresses timing and assumes the other transfer eligibility requirements are met. DHS may extend the OPT I-539 exemption beyond March 18 in six-month increments by Federal Register notification; no such extension was located as of November 14, 2026.

Q3.answer: (a) December 13, 2026: January 12, 2027 program start − 30 days. (b) January 17, 2028: December 18, 2027 program end + 30 days. CBP determines admissibility and the actual admission. (c) Yes. An unexpected change of faculty adviser is an example of a compelling academic reason. Academic probation or suspension is one expressly unacceptable reason. (d) Yes. The DSO must enter the new end date before the end date on the most recent I-20 passes. If entered afterward, Tomás must request reinstatement; a DSO recommendation alone does not grant an extension of stay. (e) For the automatic employment extension, the conservative deadline is December 18, 2027, before the 30-day departure period begins. Receipt afterward, through January 17, 2028, is still timely for an extension application, but filing in that 30-day period does not automatically extend on-campus employment or CPT; study may continue while the timely application is pending. (f) If timely filed before that departure period, the maximum automatic employment extension is 240 days from the I-94 end date: January 17, 2028 + 240 days = September 13, 2028, or an earlier USCIS decision. Continued work remains subject to the underlying on-campus employment conditions. (g) If granted for the full new program, May 19, 2028 + 30 days = June 18, 2028. If denied after the authorized admission period expires, Tomás and any dependents must immediately depart.
